subject: research/simdesign-buckleguard
professional: a senior structural / mechanical design engineer who sizes thin steel brackets and signs off stability checks (EN 1993-1-1 6.3.2, AISC 360-22 F11 for rectangular bars, Timoshenko & Gere 1961 ch. 6), and who reviews FE-driven optimisation; first checks: the LTB closed forms and torsion constant, whether the peak-stress FE result that sets feasibility is mesh-converged at the fillet, whether the knock-down K is tied to a design code, and whether the headline mass saving survives those

evidence.correctness: Recomputed independently (`python3 /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-oss-monorepo/f59c5cce-fbdc-5341-97d2-6a5629e767ca/scratchpad/buckleguard/hand.py`, plain Python, J from Roark 7th ed. Table 10.7 with the b^4/w^4 term rather than the code's 1-0.63 b/w): governing LTB factor 3.1375 at w=8,b=2 (README/test 3.14), 0.9798 at w=6,b=1.5 (test comment 0.98), 3.5376 at the K=3 optimum (guards.txt 3.54), 6.73 / 8.06 / 17.23 at the slender, K=8 and 3 mm rows (all match). Max factor inside the bounds at b=1.5 is 4.977 at w=25 and 11.72 at b=2, so the 'infeasible for K>=5 (1.5 mm) and K=12 (2 mm)' rows are analytically certain. Mass by hand (L area + r^2(1-pi/4), times b and 7.85e-3) = tool to 0.01 g on four optima. FE tip deflection 0.252/0.330 mm lies between a rigid-corner frame bound (0.233/0.335) and a centreline frame (0.287/0.396): plausible. The failure: the peak von Mises that decides feasibility is not mesh-converged. `/usr/bin/python3.13 -I .../conv.py` on the reported optima: K=3 design (w 18.72, r 8.26, b 1.5) peak 98.7 / 111.5 / 111.5 / 112.8 MPa at h = 1.5 / 1.0 / 0.75 / 0.5 mm; old-rule design (15.61, 13.27, 2.0) 98.7 / 100.6 / 105.9 / 107.7 MPa. Both 'feasible' designs exceed the 100 MPa limit by 8-13% on a refined mesh, peak at the fillet tangency (x ~ w, y ~ w+r, `where.py`), not at the load or clamp. On h = 0.6 the old rule at 2 mm has no feasible design (w <= 16 allowed: 100.5 MPa at r 15, 102.2 at r 13), and the 3 mm row's 44.22 g design is 112.5 MPa; a 3 mm design at 46.7 g (w 13.3, r 12) passes at 98.0, while 1.5 mm passes at 32.6 g (w 19.5, r 12, 96.7 MPa). So on a converged mesh the old rule costs about 30%, not 12%: the direction of the headline holds, its number does not.
evidence.completeness: Everything the README says was run exists: package, 7 tests, experiments/guards.py with guards.txt/json (json is 1,752 bytes on one line, not empty), sensitivity.py with sensitivity.txt/json. Reran sensitivity.py in a scratch copy of the project (`cd .../scratchpad/buckleguard/copy && python3.13 -I experiments/sensitivity.py`), output identical to the committed sensitivity.txt in 1 min 6 s on 4 cores. guards.py (8 min) not rerun; its four optima re-evaluated with evaluate() at h=1.5 reproduce mass, peak and factor to the printed digits. The 'w <= 12 at b = 1.5 gives 227-266 MPa' claim reproduced: 265.6/229.4/226.8 MPa at r = 4/8/12. Live page https://marisstella.app/research/simdesign-buckleguard/ returns 200 and repeats the README result. No stubs or TODOs.
evidence.verification: `cd research/simdesign-buckleguard && python3.13 -m pytest -q tests`: 7 passed in 0.57 s. The tests cover only the guard switch and the LTB closed form. Five seeded mutants via platform/ci/quality_mutate.py: 1 caught (vertical-arm pi/(2H) -> pi/H), 4 survived: horizontal-arm length (L-w)^2 -> L^2, MAX_SLENDER 8 -> 12, von Mises 3*sxy^2 -> sxy^2, clamp-zone exclusion removed. No test touches the FE solve, the stress measure, evaluate() or the optimiser, i.e. everything the headline mass numbers come from; nothing checks mesh convergence, which is where the real defect is.
evidence.craft: Read model.py, ltb.py, dfm.py, optimise.py, measures.py, __init__.py, tests, both experiment scripts. ltb.py is short, clear and documents its assumptions. Defects: model.py:105-107 dead code (`... if False else None`, and an `fb` assigned twice and never used); model.py:18 Material default still documented as an FDM thermoplastic in a steel-sheet project; configuration through mutable module globals (dfm.GUARD, dfm.BUCKLE_MIN) set inside worker processes and reset in tearDown, fragile but works; the whole package is a copy of simdesign-widerweb (the chain has 20+ near-identical copies, PROGRAMMES.md:8-14), so a fix in one never reaches the others. The FE peak is sampled at P2 element centroids on a 1.5 mm grid mesh with no boundary refinement at the fillet, which is why it under-reads.
evidence.claims: Backed: every number in the results table and sensitivity bullets against guards.txt/sensitivity.txt; the 227-266 MPa claim; the 3.14 webbuckle factor; 'the guard does not bind at K=3' (optimum factors 3.44-3.56 > 3); disclosures (stylised, AI-assisted, one mesh, not a recommendation to cut). Not backed: the headline 'the old rule cost about 12% of mass' (README:36, page, research/README.md:575) is a coarse-mesh number; on h <= 1.0 both compared designs violate the stated 100 MPa limit and the old-rule 2 mm design does not exist, which the project's own ancestor simdesign-meshconverge already reported (empty feasible set at 2 mm, w <= 16, on h = 1.0 and 0.5). The 'one mesh' limitation is disclosed but its known consequence is not. README:43 calls the K>=5 / K=12 infeasibility 'not a proof' when it follows in closed form from the factor's maximum at w=25 (an under-claim). README 'about 12%': the table gives 12.3-13.7%.
evidence.fitness: Job for a researcher: take the guard and the mass price of the old rule into the next step. The LTB piece is reusable (and simdesign-loadbind did build on it). The mass result is not safe to build on without rerunning at h <= 0.75. Nearest prior work: elastic LTB of narrow rectangular cantilevers (Timoshenko & Gere 1961 sec. 6.2-6.3; Trahair, Flexural-Torsional Buckling of Structures, 1993) and design-code LTB checks for rectangular bars (AISC 360-22 F11; EN 1993-1-1 6.3.2), plus stability-constrained structural optimisation (e.g. topology optimisation with buckling constraints, Ferrari & Sigmund 2019). Against that, replacing a w/b rule with an elastic LTB factor is textbook practice, not a new result; it is one small step in a 20+-project chain that PROGRAMMES.md itself calls below thesis level. Not PhD level, not publishable as is.
evidence.domain: The closed forms are the right ones (cantilever end couple M_cr = pi/(2l) sqrt(EIy GJ); tip load at centroid P_cr = 4.013 sqrt(EIy GJ)/l^2; thin-rectangle J), and the README is candid that imperfections, residual stress, corner flexibility, the lever-applied (non-axial) end moment and local crippling are absent. Departures a senior engineer raises: (1) K = 3 is 'a guess at a knock-down' when the codes give one: my EN 1993-1-1 6.3.2.2 check of the K=3 optimum (S235 assumed, curve d, `python3 .../codes.py`) gives lambda_LT 0.908, chi 0.516, utilisation 0.66 at working load; AISC F11 (Lb d/t^2 = 666 or 1331 with Lb = l or 2l) gives Mn/My 1.31/1.09, ASD utilisation 0.44/0.53, so the design passes both and the code check would have replaced the arbitrary K and its sensitivity sweep. (2) Feasibility rests on an unconverged peak stress at a fillet (correctness above); a stress engineer would check convergence before quoting a saving. (3) Arm-by-arm cantilever idealisation ignores the corner's torsional flexibility (unconservative, disclosed) and the stabilising axial tension (conservative, disclosed).

defects.what: Feasibility rests on a peak von Mises stress that is not mesh-converged: the reported K=3 optimum reads 98.7 MPa at h=1.5 but 111.5-112.8 MPa at h=1.0-0.5, the old-rule optimum 98.7 -> 107.7 MPa, both over the 100 MPa limit (peak at the fillet tangency). On h=0.6 the old rule has no feasible 2 mm design (w<=16 gives >=100.5 MPa) and is pushed to 3 mm (about 46.7 g) against about 32.6 g at 1.5 mm, so the headline '12% lighter' is about 30% on a converged mesh. The project's own ancestor simdesign-meshconverge had already reported the empty 2 mm feasible set at h=1.0 and 0.5.

Headline claim 'the old rule cost about 12% of mass' (README, live page, research/README.md index) is a coarse-mesh artefact; the 'one mesh' limitation is disclosed but its known consequence (from simdesign-meshconverge/meshmargin) is not.

No test touches the FE solve, the stress measure, evaluate() or the optimiser; 4 of 5 seeded mutants survive (von Mises shear term, clamp-zone exclusion, MAX_SLENDER, horizontal-arm length), and nothing checks mesh convergence.

K = 3 is described as a guess and swept, while design codes give the answer for this section: EN 1993-1-1 6.3.2.2 (curve d) gives utilisation 0.66 and AISC 360-22 F11 0.44-0.53 for the 1.5 mm optimum (S235 assumed). Neither code nor Trahair is cited.

README calls the K>=5 (1.5 mm) and K=12 (2 mm) infeasibility 'what a stochastic search found, not a proof', but it follows in closed form: the factor is monotone in w and peaks at 4.98 and 11.72 at the w=25 bound.
Dead code in the solver: a boundary basis built under `if False` and a second `fb` that is never used.

Material dataclass default documented as an FDM thermoplastic in a steel-sheet project (the copied package carries all four processes); the whole package is a copy of simdesign-widerweb, so fixes do not propagate.

verdict: The buckling arithmetic is right: an independent implementation of the Timoshenko-Gere cantilever formulas reproduces every LTB factor in the tables (3.14, 0.98, 3.54, 6.73, 8.06, 17.23), masses match a hand area to 0.01 g, FE deflection sits between frame bounds, and the K>=5 infeasibility is certain in closed form. The result the project exists for is not: feasibility is decided by a peak fillet stress read on a 1.5 mm mesh, and on h <= 1.0 both compared optima exceed the 100 MPa limit by 8-13%; the old rule's 2 mm design vanishes (as the chain's own simdesign-meshconverge had shown), so the saving is about 30%, not 12%. The direction of the conclusion holds. Tests pin only the closed form (4 of 5 core mutants survive), K=3 is guessed where EN 1993-1-1 and AISC F11 give a check (which the 1.5 mm design passes), and the step is textbook practice, far from the PhD bar. Below the bar on correctness, verification and claims.
